title: Packages: where they come from and which version you have

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A package is a collection of R functions, data and documentation that extends what base R, the set of standard packages installed with R itself, can do.

Installing a package, with install.packages(), downloads it from a repository such as CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network) and stores it on the computer. It is done once per computer, and again only to change the version. Loading a package, with library(), makes its functions available in the current R session (R from the moment it starts until it is closed or restarted). install.packages() and packageVersion() need the name in quotation marks; library() also accepts it without.

Every package has a version number, read with packageVersion(). R itself has one, held in R.version.string. A package’s behaviour, and the messages it prints, can change between versions.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
A package is a bundle of functions, with the help pages that explain them and sometimes some data. Most are kept on CRAN, a set of websites from which R downloads them.

Using a package takes two steps, and they happen at different times.

First, install it, once per computer. You type it in the console, not in your script:

install.packages("dplyr")

Then load it, in every session. It goes at the top of your script:

library(dplyr)

Some packages share a function name with another package. Loading dplyr, for example, hides another filter(), which belongs to stats, a package that comes with R. To be sure which one you get, write the package name and two colons in front: dplyr::filter() or stats::filter().

The tidyverse is a family of packages: loading it loads nine, among them dplyr and readr.

Packages change. Each has a version number, and so does R. Check yours with:

R.version.string
packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] "R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29)"
[1] ‘1.1.4’

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start a fresh R session (in RStudio, Session, then Restart R) and try a function from dplyr before loading it. n_distinct() counts how many different values a vector holds. Here it is given the home districts of four made-up clinic patients:

n_distinct(c("Raipur", "Durg", "Raipur", "Bilaspur"))
Error in n_distinct(c("Raipur", "Durg", "Raipur", "Bilaspur")) :
  could not find function "n_distinct"

R looked through everything loaded and found no function by that name. The package is installed, but the session has not been told to use it. This is a common error in a script that worked yesterday: yesterday’s session had loaded the package, and today’s has not. Load it:

library(dplyr)

Attaching package: ‘dplyr’

The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

Read the message. “Masked” means hidden. dplyr has functions called filter() and lag(), and so does stats. It also has four functions whose names are already used in base. From now on in this session, filter means dplyr’s filter(). Now the call works:

n_distinct(c("Raipur", "Durg", "Raipur", "Bilaspur"))
[1] 3

Three different districts. To see the order R searches in, ask for the search list:

search()
 [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:dplyr"     "package:stats"
 [4] "package:graphics"  "package:grDevices" "package:utils"
 [7] "package:datasets"  "package:methods"   "Autoloads"
[10] "package:base"

.GlobalEnv is the workspace, where the objects you make are kept, and R looks there first. dplyr now comes before stats, which is why its filter() wins.

The two-colon form needs no library() call at all. It names the package and the function together. Read the practice file and count its rows, using readr without loading it. Two new pieces appear here. here::here() builds the path to the file from the top of your project, which section 7 sets up; if you have none yet, run this after that section. show_col_types = FALSE turns off a report that read_csv() prints, which the section on reading files explains. nrow() counts the rows of a table:

readr::read_csv(here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  nrow()
[1] 344

The file has 344 rows. One row is one adult penguin’s record on one sampling expedition, a nesting observation; the same bird can appear in more than one row. The two-colon form is useful when you need one function from a package once. When a script uses a package throughout, load it with library() at the top, so a reader sees at once what the script needs.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The district names are made up. The search list printed here is the one from a fresh session in this book’s setup. Yours will list more if you load more packages, and RStudio may show extra entries.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Here is the failure that versions cause. A script written two years ago uses a function that a newer version of a package has changed. The script stops with an error, or, worse, runs and prints something slightly different. Nothing in the script tells you which version it was written for.

So record the versions. Ask for the version of R and of each package your script loads:

R.version.string
packageVersion("dplyr")
packageVersion("readr")
[1] "R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29)"
[1] ‘1.1.4’
[1] ‘2.1.5’

These are the versions behind every output in this book: R 4.3.3, dplyr 1.1.4 and readr 2.1.5. They are not the newest. When this book was written (checked 2 October 2026), R 4.6.1 (June 2026) and dplyr 1.2.0 (February 2026) had been released. The dplyr 1.2.0 changelog, the list of what changed in that version, adds new functions and, among other changes, now requires R 4.1.0 or later.

For you this means two things. First, if your output differs from the book’s in a message or a small detail, compare your versions with the book’s before you suspect your code. Second, your own script should say which versions it ran on. packageVersion() returns a version, not plain text, so R compares it with the text part by part, as numbers:

packageVersion("dplyr") >= "1.1.0"
[1] TRUE

Printing the versions at the end of every script, in one line, is the subject of a later section on running a script from top to bottom.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: A version number tells you which release you have, not what changed between releases. For that you read the package’s changelog. Even with the same versions, a different operating system can, rarely, give a different result.

points.html: The error is to put install.packages() in your script. Install once, in the console.
“could not find function” means R has no function by that name loaded. Check the spelling, then check that its package is loaded in this session.
Read the message that library() prints. After library(dplyr), filter() means dplyr’s.
Record the version of R and of every package your analysis loads, in the script’s output.
When a trainee’s output differs from the book’s in a message or a detail, have them compare versions with packageVersion() before they rewrite their code.
A version number names a release. It does not pin it: the next person to run install.packages() gets whatever version is current that day.

blocks.prompt: You are starting a script, analysis.R, that will read a raw file with readr and reshape it with dplyr. Write its first lines: the packages it needs and a record of the versions it ran on. Say why install.packages() does not appear in it.
blocks.answer:
One version:

# Packages: installed once per computer with install.packages(), loaded here
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)  # hides the masking message shown above

# Versions this script ran on
R.version.string
packageVersion("readr")
packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] "R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29)"
[1] ‘2.1.5’
[1] ‘1.1.4’

install.packages() is not in the script because installing is done once per computer, in the console. In a script it would download the package on every run, need an internet connection, and quietly change the version for anyone who ran it. The library() lines at the top tell a reader at once which packages the script needs. The version lines record what it ran on, so a later difference can be traced to a version and not to the code.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, say how often you run install.packages() and how often you run library(), and where each one goes.
blocks.answer: install.packages() once per computer, typed in the console. library() in every session that uses the package, at the top of the script.

blocks.prompt: Write the line you would type in the console to install the package readr. Then write the line that goes at the top of a script that uses it.
blocks.answer:
In the console, once per computer:

install.packages("readr")

At the top of the script:

library(readr)

readr prints nothing when it loads. Silence means it worked.

blocks.prompt: In a fresh session you load dplyr and then type filter(...). Which package’s filter() runs? Write the call you would use to run the other one, and the line that shows you what dplyr hides when it loads.
blocks.answer:
dplyr’s filter() runs, because dplyr was attached after stats and masks it. The other is called as stats::filter(). The line that shows the masking is the library() call itself:

library(dplyr)

Attaching package: ‘dplyr’

The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

The message lists filter among the objects masked from package:stats.

blocks.prompt: Write the lines that print the version of R you are running and the version of the package here.
blocks.answer:
R.version.string
packageVersion("here")
[1] "R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29)"
[1] ‘1.0.1’

This book’s outputs were made with these versions. Yours may be newer.

blocks.prompt: Without loading any package, count the rows of penguins_raw.csv in your project’s data-raw folder, and say what one row stands for. (The project is set up in section 7; if you have none yet, do this after it.)
blocks.answer:
readr::read_csv(here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  nrow()
[1] 344

readr:: and here:: call each function from its package without library(). The file has 344 rows. One row is one adult penguin’s record on one sampling expedition; the same bird can appear in more than one row.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague’s script begins as below and stops at its second line with the error shown. The script worked for them yesterday. Find what broke.

raw <- here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv")
penguins_raw <- read_csv(raw, show_col_types = FALSE)
Error in read_csv(raw, show_col_types = FALSE) :
  could not find function "read_csv"
blocks.answer:
read_csv() belongs to readr, and the script never loads readr. Yesterday the colleague had loaded it by hand in the console, so the session knew the function. Today’s fresh session does not. Add the library() line at the top:

library(readr)
raw <- here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv")
penguins_raw <- read_csv(raw, show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(penguins_raw)
[1] 344

The script now reads the file’s 344 rows. A script must load everything it uses. Whatever happened in the console earlier does not count.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants to report the version of dplyr. Their line and its error are below. Find what broke, and say why the mistake is easy to make.

packageVersion(dplyr)
Error: object 'dplyr' not found
blocks.answer:
packageVersion() takes the package’s name as text, in quotation marks. Without them, R looks for an object called dplyr, and there is none.

packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] ‘1.1.4’

The mistake is easy to make because library(dplyr) works without quotation marks, so the two calls look as though they should take the same form. They do not: library() is written to accept a bare name, and most functions are not.

blocks.prompt: A made-up thesis methods section says: “All analyses were carried out in R.” Write the lines that would record what this sentence leaves out, for an analysis that uses readr and dplyr. Run them, and say what even your fuller record does not establish.
blocks.answer:
R.version.string
packageVersion("readr")
packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] "R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29)"
[1] ‘2.1.5’
[1] ‘1.1.4’

A fuller sentence: “All analyses were carried out in R version 4.3.3 with readr 2.1.5 and dplyr 1.1.4.”

What the fuller record does not establish:

  • That the analysis gives the same numbers on newer versions. It records what was used, not what would happen with something else.
  • That these are the only packages involved. Packages that load other packages, and the operating system, are not listed. A complete record comes later, in the section on running a script from top to bottom.
  • That the code is correct. Recorded versions make a wrong analysis repeatable, not right.
